article.title: A provider stopped accepting traffic
article.excerpt: Telling an account-level failure apart from a bad route, and what failover can and cannot absorb for you.

p: Failures rise suddenly and cluster: sends that went through fine yesterday now come back rejected, while a second connected account keeps working. That contrast is the signal — the problem is attached to one connection, not to your content.

list: Naming the credentials — the account-level problem. Something changed on the provider side: a rotated key, a suspended account, a quota exhausted.
Naming the sender — the sender identity is no longer authorized. Registration, verification or a carrier filter is the likely cause, and it is resolved with the provider.
Naming the destination — the route to a country or network is refusing this sender type. Every account may hit the same wall, so failover will not help.

sections.h: What failover does, and what it does not
p: Automatic failover moves traffic to another connected account on the SMS channel, which absorbs an account-level failure without you intervening. It cannot absorb a route-level failure: if the rejection is attached to the destination rather than to the account, there is nothing for failover to route around.
sections.note: Automatic failover between connected accounts is implemented for the SMS channel and is not claimed for the email or WhatsApp channels.

steps.h: Read the error codes per connection
steps.p: The log records the provider’s raw error. Compare a failing account against a working one.

steps.h: See whether failures cluster by destination
steps.p: Clustered by destination points at a route or a registration; spread across destinations points at the account.
If another account is carrying the volume, failover is working and your remaining task is the account that failed.

steps.h: Fix the underlying cause with the provider
steps.p: The platform cannot lift a carrier filter, restore a suspended account or renew a registration.
